title: The widow of Naim (Luke 7:11–17)
hook: Jesus stops a funeral because he had compassion on the mother

segments.voice: Yesterday, love your enemies, and a measure of grain pressed down and spilling over. Your line was good measure. Where did you let it spill? Day four hundred fifty-five, the end of a week.

Two crowds meet at a town gate. One is coming out: a funeral. In that world the dead were buried quickly, often the same day, and the procession walked out past the gate with mourners wailing. On the bier is a young man, the only son of his mother, and she is a widow. One crowd going out with death. The other crowd is coming in, following Jesus and his disciples up the road. The town is Naim, a small place in Galilee. Nobody asks Jesus for anything. Today, what he does anyway.
screen: `TWO CROWDS AT A TOWN GATE.` → `AN ONLY SON, A WIDOWED MOTHER.` → `NOBODY ASKS.`

segments.voice: Luke tells it in six verses. Here's the turning point: "And when the Lord had seen her, being moved with mercy towards her, he said to her: Weep not." Look at the order. He sees her first. Not the dead son, the mother. Luke wants us to understand what this means for her: a widow who has lost her only son has lost her family, and in that world often her protection and her living too. Then he's moved. Luke's Greek word for it comes from the word for the inner organs, the gut. It's the feeling that grabs you in the stomach. Then he speaks to her, two words: weep not. Only then does he touch the bier, and the bearers stop. "Young man, I say to thee, arise." The young man sits up and begins to speak, and Luke adds the gentlest line in the story: he delivered him to his mother. Not to the crowd. To her. The people's reaction is fear and praise. They say a great prophet has risen among us, and God has visited his people. They're thinking of Elijah, who raised a widow's son at Sarephta centuries before, in the Third Book of Kings in the Douay. Luke is the only Gospel that tells this story, and he notices widows again and again: Anna in the Temple, the widow who won't stop knocking on a judge's door, the widow with two small coins. Catholics hear it as a picture of how God looks at grief. Before anything is fixed, someone sees you, and is moved, and speaks to you. Weep not isn't a scolding. It's what you say to a person when you're about to help.
screen: `HE SEES THE MOTHER FIRST.` · `MOVED IN THE GUT.` · `YOUNG MAN, ARISE.` · `HE GAVE HIM TO HIS MOTHER.` · then, large: `WEEP NOT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: comfort someone grieving. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone you know who is grieving right now: a death, a divorce, a diagnosis, a child far away. Picture them the way Jesus saw the widow at the gate. Let yourself feel it in the gut. Then decide on one small thing you'll do for them today: a message, a meal, sitting with them, saying the name of the one they lost. If you pray, hold them before God. The bell holds the time.
The widow of Naim. A mother at a town gate with her only son on the bier, seen first and comforted by Jesus before anyone asked. Today's word.

Your line: weep not. Today, reach out to one grieving person. And that's week sixty-five: two coats, the son of Adam, Nazareth, depart from me, blessed are you poor, love your enemies, and Naim. Day four hundred fifty-five.
screen: `WEEK SIXTY-FIVE: COATS · ADAM · NAZARETH · THE CATCH · THE POOR · ENEMIES · NAIM`

howItsDone: Comforting the sorrowful is one of the Church's spiritual works of mercy, and Catholic parishes often send people to sit with grieving families, bring meals, and pray with them at the funeral vigil.

fork.setup: you're walking into a town and meet a funeral coming out. a widow is following her only son's body. nobody has asked you for anything. what do you do?
options: step aside respectfully and let them pass.
speak to the mother first: weep not.
fork.reveal: he speaks to her before he does anything else, then touches the bier and raises her son, and gives him back to her.

original.note: Greek: he was moved with compassion, from splanchna, the inner organs: mercy felt in the gut.

trapdoor: what you thought: weep not means stop crying, you're overreacting.
what it means: Jesus sees the widow, is moved, and says weep not as the first word of comfort before he raises her son.
what a scholar hears: esplanchnisthe, from splanchna, the gut; in the Gospels the verb is used only of Jesus or of figures in his parables.
